item.research_question: What are the high-temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy superalloy (HESA) with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, and how do they compare to conventional superalloys and other HEAs?
item.processing_route: Vacuum-arc-melting followed by directional-solidification; solution-heat-treatment at 1210 °C for 10 h; primary aging at 1000 °C for 3 h; secondary aging at 800 °C for 20 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests at strain rate 10^-3 sec^-1 from room temperature to 950 °C; creep tests at 750, 850, and 982 °C under constant stress of 159 MPa
key_findings: The HESA possesses a γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates with an average size of 290 nm and 69 vol% after heat treatment.
The γ′ solvus temperature is 1199 °C and the solidus temperature is 1276 °C.
The lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ′ at 982 °C is calculated to be 0.08%.
The estimated stacking fault energy (SFE) of the HESA matrix is approximately 0.7 J/m², which is lower than that of CMSX-2.
The anti-phase boundary (APB) energy of the γ′ phase in HESA is 0.22 J/m², higher than the 0.19 J/m² in CMSX-2.
The creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C is about 114 hours, comparable to first-generation Ni-based superalloys like Rene′ 80.
The creep activation energy (Q) for HESA is estimated to be 290 kJ/mol, higher than the 230 kJ/mol for CMSX-2.
At 982 °C, the γ′ precipitates undergo parallel rafting (P-raft) along the stress axis, coarsening from 0.29 μm to 0.5 μm perpendicular and extending to 3 μm parallel to the stress.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the high strength to the high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates, low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, and high anti-phase boundary energy of the precipitates. For creep, the authors argue that the lower SFE and higher activation energy contribute to lower creep rates at intermediate temperatures by making dislocation bowing more difficult. At 982 °C, the positive lattice misfit leads to parallel rafting, which the authors state causes the creep curves to be dominated by tertiary creep behavior, unlike the perpendicular rafting seen in CMSX-2.
item.limitations: The authors note that the current γ′ size of 290 nm is smaller than the estimated optimized size of 390 nm for peak strength, suggesting the strength could be increased by 16% with larger precipitates. They also mention that the positive temperature dependence on yield strength is less pronounced compared to CMSX-2.
item.future_work: The authors propose studying the non-isothermal creep behavior of HESA and suggest that minor additions of γ partitioning elements like Mo and Re could lead to desirable negative lattice misfit for N-type rafting and provide solid-solution strengthening.
quotes: The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures
Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C
The creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior

Question: What are the high-temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy superalloy (HESA) with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, and how do they compare to conventional superalloys and other HEAs?. System: Ni47.9Al10.2Co16.9Cr7.4Fe8.9Ti5.8Mo0.9Nb1.2W0.4C0.4 (at%) high entropy superalloy (HESA). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting followed by directional-solidification; solution-heat-treatment at 1210 °C for 10 h; primary aging at 1000 °C for 3 h; secondary aging at 800 °C for 20 h. Test conditions: Tensile tests at strain rate 10^-3 sec^-1 from room temperature to 950 °C; creep tests at 750, 850, and 982 °C under constant stress of 159 MPa. Findings: The HESA possesses a γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates with an average size of 290 nm and 69 vol% after heat treatment.; The γ′ solvus temperature is 1199 °C and the solidus temperature is 1276 °C.; The lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ′ at 982 °C is calculated to be 0.08%.; The estimated stacking fault energy (SFE) of the HESA matrix is approximately 0.7 J/m², which is lower than that of CMSX-2.; The anti-phase boundary (APB) energy of the γ′ phase in HESA is 0.22 J/m², higher than the 0.19 J/m² in CMSX-2.; The creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C is about 114 hours, comparable to first-generation Ni-based superalloys like Rene′ 80.; The creep activation energy (Q) for HESA is estimated to be 290 kJ/mol, higher than the 230 kJ/mol for CMSX-2.; At 982 °C, the γ′ precipitates undergo parallel rafting (P-raft) along the stress axis, coarsening from 0.29 μm to 0.5 μm perpendicular and extending to 3 μm parallel to the stress.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the high strength to the high volume fraction of γ′ precipitates, low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, and high anti-phase boundary energy of the precipitates. For creep, the authors argue that the lower SFE and higher activation energy contribute to lower creep rates at intermediate temperatures by making dislocation bowing more difficult. At 982 °C, the positive lattice misfit leads to parallel rafting, which the authors state causes the creep curves to be dominated by tertiary creep behavior, unlike the perpendicular rafting seen in CMSX-2.. Limitations: The authors note that the current γ′ size of 290 nm is smaller than the estimated optimized size of 390 nm for peak strength, suggesting the strength could be increased by 16% with larger precipitates. They also mention that the positive temperature dependence on yield strength is less pronounced compared to CMSX-2.. Future work: The authors propose studying the non-isothermal creep behavior of HESA and suggest that minor additions of γ partitioning elements like Mo and Re could lead to desirable negative lattice misfit for N-type rafting and provide solid-solution strengthening..
